documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
4 Questions, 60 minutes

**INSTRUCTIONS**

**DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN**

- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example,

  Doe, Jamie

  Q1 – 1/3
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Each of the four questions is worth 25 points. The questions are not necessarily of the same difficulty.

Binomial expansion $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for $|x| \ll 1$

(will not be provided on the second screening exam)

| | |
|---|---|

| Sphere | $\frac{2}{5} MR^2$ |
| Rod | $\frac{1}{12} ML^2$ |

documentNotes.title: Authors
documentNotes.statement: *The 2002 Preliminary Examination open response questions were written by the coaches of the United States Physics Team. The coaches are: Academic Director, Mary Mogge – Professor of Physics at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona, CA; Senior Coach, Leaf Turner – Physicist in the Theoretical Division of Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos, NM; Warren Turner – Physics Teacher at Massachusetts Academy of Math and Science, Worcester, MA; Robert Shurtz – Physics Teacher at the Hawken School, Gates Mills, OH. Questions 1 and 3 were suggested by Warren Turner, Question 2 by Mary Mogge, and Question 4 by Leaf Turner.*

documentNotes.title: Solutions to Problems
documentNotes.statement: *Any correct solution should be awarded equivalent points. Suggested partial-credit points are presented in square brackets at the right margin. You may further break down the listed points into one point increments. If it is clear they have done an intermediate step, they should get credit for it even if they have not presented it. For example, in 1.a., if a student wrote down $mgH = Fh$, they should get 9 points credit. Students should not be penalized in a subsequent part for using the wrong answer to a previous part. (No double jeopardy.)*

The problems PDF uses a symbol font that renders some glyphs wrongly in the page image: the bullets appear as “∞”, “(1 + x)^n ⊕ 1 + nx” is “≈” (text layer), “∅x” in problem 3 is “∆x” (text layer), and “45ϒ” in problem 4 is “45°” (text layer); these are transcribed as the intended characters. Problem 1 has no figure. Problem 3 shows two diagrams (a close-up of the glider with v_o and the glider on the incline), cropped separately because body text sits beside the close-up. The solutions PDF is a scan without a text layer. In solution 3a the subscript of “ma_x” is faint in the scan and read as x from context. In solution 4 the last line prints “θ ≤ tan⁻¹(x_cg/L) − tan⁻¹(1/3) = 0.32 radians = 18.4°”: the minus sign between the arctangents is evidently a misprint for “=”; kept as printed (mathematics is never changed) and noted in the answer. No text fixes were needed.

problems.statement: A rocket of mass $m$ is launched straight up, reaches a maximum height $H$ above the ground, and begins its vertical descent. The rocket is in free fall until it falls to a height $h$. At that point, the rocket’s engines are fired and provide a continuous upward thrust $F$. You may neglect the following: air resistance; any horizontal motion of the rocket; and any change in the mass of the rocket. Express your answers in terms of only the variables given ($H$, $F$, $m$) and, if necessary, the gravitational field at the Earth’s surface $g$ and the radius of the Earth $R_E$.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: $H$ is small enough that the force of gravity is constant during the flight of the rocket. At what height $h$ above the surface of the Earth should the engines be fired so that the rocket lands safely with zero velocity?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: For what values of $F$ is a zero velocity landing impossible?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: $H$ is large enough that the force of gravity is not constant during the flight of the rocket. At what height $h$ above the surface of the Earth should the engines be fired so that the rocket lands safely with zero velocity?

solution.statement:
**1. a.** Using the work-energy theorem $\mathrm{PE}_i + \mathrm{KE}_i + W = \mathrm{PE}_f + \mathrm{KE}_f$ **[1]**

“i” refers to the point of maximum height $H$ and “f” refers to the Earth’s surface. At both points the kinetic energy is zero

$\mathrm{KE}_i = 0 \qquad \mathrm{KE}_f = 0.$ **[2]**

Setting the potential energy at the Earth’s surface equal to zero

$\mathrm{PE}_i = mgH \qquad \mathrm{PE}_f = 0.$ **[2]**

The work done by the constant force F $\quad W = \vec{F}\cdot\vec{d}$ **[1]**

$\vec{F}$ is upward, displacement $\vec{d}$ is downward and has magnitude $h$. $\quad W = -Fh.$ **[2]**

Inserting these into the work energy equation $\quad mgH - Fh = 0$ **[1]**

or

$$h = \frac{mg}{F}H.$$ **[1]**

**b.** A zero velocity solution is impossible if $h \ge H$. Then **[2]**

$$H \le \frac{mg}{F}H,$$ **[1]**

or

$$F \le mg.$$ **[2]**

*$\{$Minus one point if $<$ instead of $\le$.$\}$ $\{$A check of the equality shows that for $h = H$, $F = mg$. So at the highest point its velocity is zero and the net force is zero. It just stays there and will not reach ground with zero velocity. This argument is not required for full credit.$\}$*

**c.** Using the work-energy theorem $\mathrm{PE}_i + \mathrm{KE}_i + W = \mathrm{PE}_f + \mathrm{KE}_f$

“i” refers to the point of maximum height $H$ and “f” refers to the Earth’s surface. At both points the kinetic energy is zero

$\mathrm{KE}_i = 0 \qquad \mathrm{KE}_f = 0.$ **[1]**

Here the gravitational potential energy is $\quad PE_i = -\dfrac{GM_E m}{R_E + H} \qquad PE_f = -\dfrac{GM_E m}{R_E}.$ **[2]**

Where $M_E$ is the mass of the Earth. The work done is $\quad W = -Fh$ **[2]**

(see above). Inserting these into the work energy equation

$$-\frac{GM_E m}{R_E + H} - Fh = -\frac{GM_E m}{R_E}$$ **[1]**

solving for $h$

$$h = \frac{GM_E m}{F}\left(\frac{1}{R_E} - \frac{1}{R_E + H}\right) = \frac{GM_E m}{F}\left(\frac{R_E + H - R_E}{R_E(R_E + H)}\right) = \frac{GM_E mH}{FR_E(R_E + H)}.$$ **[1]**

Answer must be expressed in terms of $m$, $H$, $F$, $g$, and $R_E$. Need to eliminate $G$ and $M_E$.

$$g = \frac{GM_E}{R_E^{\,2}}$$ **[1]**

Solving for $\quad GM_E = gR_E^{\,2}.$ **[1]**

Inserting this into the equation for $h$

$$h = \frac{\left(gR_E^{\,2}\right)mH}{FR_E(R_E + H)} = \frac{mgHR_E}{F(R_E + H)} = \frac{mg}{F}H\left(\frac{1}{1 + H/R_E}\right).$$ **[1]**

problems.statement: A particle of mass $m$ is constrained to move in one dimension. A force $\mathbf{F}$ acts on the particle. $\mathbf{F}$ always points toward the position labeled $E$. For example, when the particle is to the left of $E$, $\mathbf{F}$ points to the right. The magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$ is a constant $F$ except at point $E$ where it is zero.

figures.alt: A horizontal line with a particle m drawn as a black dot to the left of a vertical tick marked E; a grey arrow labelled A points from the tick at E leftwards to above the particle, showing the displacement A.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: The system is horizontal. $\mathbf{F}$ is the net force acting on the particle. The particle is displaced a distance $A$ from the equilibrium position $E$ and released from rest. What is the period of the motion?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: The system is vertical. Both the force $\mathbf{F}$ described above and gravity act on the system. The particle is displaced a distance $A$ above the position $E$ and released from rest. $F > mg$. What is the period of the motion?

solution.statement:
**2. a.** When the particle is released, it begins to move with an acceleration which has magnitude

$$a = \frac{F}{m}$$ **[2]**

and is directed toward position $E$. Since it starts from rest $\quad A = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ **[2]**

It reaches $E$ in time $t$

$$t = \sqrt{\frac{2A}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F}}$$ **[1]**

The particle oscillates back and forth between amplitude A on the right and A on the left. **[2]**

The time for one complete cycle is four times this $\quad T = 4t$ **[2]**

$$T = 4\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F}}$$ **[1]**

**b.** The particle oscillates between amplitude $A$ above point $E$ and $A'$ below. $A \ne A'$ **[1]**

Let $t_1$ = time it takes the particle to go from amplitude $A$ above to point $E$ and from $E$ up to $A$.

Let $t_2$ = time it takes the particle to go from point $E$ to amplitude $A'$ below and from $A'$ up to $E$.

The period is $\quad T = 2t_1 + 2t_2$ **[2]**

When the particle is above point E, the net force acting on it is

$$ma = \sum F = F + mg \quad \text{downward.}$$ **[1]**

The magnitude of the acceleration is $\quad a = \dfrac{F + mg}{m}$ **[1]**

Starting from rest the particle travels a distance $A$ given by $\quad A = \tfrac{1}{2}at_1^{\,2}$ **[1]**

Solving for $t_1$

$$t_1 = \sqrt{\frac{2A}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}$$ **[1]**

The particle passes through E with velocity

$$v_E = at_1 = \left(\frac{F + mg}{m}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}$$ **[1]**

When the particle is below point E, the net force acting on it is

$$ma = \sum F = F - mg \quad \text{upward}$$ **[1]**

The magnitude of the acceleration is $\quad a = \dfrac{F - mg}{m}$ **[1]**

It reaches maximum downward displacement $A'$ when $v = 0$. **[1]**

$$v = 0 = v_E - at_2$$ **[1]**

Solving for $t_2$

$$t_2 = \frac{v_E}{a} = \left(\frac{F + mg}{m}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}\left(\frac{m}{F - mg}\right) = \left(\frac{F + mg}{F - mg}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}$$ **[1]**

$$T = 2t_1 + 2t_2 = 2\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}} + 2\left(\frac{F + mg}{F - mg}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}$$ **[1]**

$$T = 2\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}\left(1 + \frac{F + mg}{F - mg}\right) = \left(\frac{4F}{F - mg}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2Am}{F + mg}}$$ **[1]**

problems.statement: An air track glider is fitted with a launcher that fires a projectile with velocity $v_{\mathrm{o}}$ perpendicular to the glider. The launch point LP is marked on the glider, as shown in the diagrams. The glider is placed on a very long air track, which is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. With the air turned on, the system can be considered frictionless. With the air turned off, the coefficient of friction between the track and glider is $\mu$. The projectile is launched at the instant the glider has velocity $v$ down the track and lands a distance $x$ down the track. While the projectile is in the air, the point LP moves a distance $x_{\mathrm{LP}}$. What is $\Delta x = x - x_{\mathrm{LP}}$, if:

figures.alt: Close-up of the glider: a rectangular block labelled LP with a launcher tube on top containing a small circle; a grey arrow labelled v_o points straight up from the tube.

The glider (a rectangle with the launcher tube and launch point LP) sitting on a straight track inclined downward to the right; the angle θ between the track and a horizontal line is marked at the lower right. The lower edge of the close-up drawing of the glider (label LP) shows at the top right.

solution.statement:
**3. a.** Selecting the $x$-axis parallel to the inclined plane and $y$-axis perpendicular to it, the forces acting on the glider are shown as components to the right. Since the glider has no acceleration in the $y$-direction (perpendicular to the plane),

$$F_N = mg\cos\theta$$ **[2]**

The acceleration in the $x$-direction can be obtained from Newton’s second law. $\quad \sum F = ma$ **[2]**

$$ma_x = mg\sin\theta - f_k$$ **[1]**

Subbing in for friction $\quad f_k = \mu F_N = \mu mg\cos\theta$ **[1]**

$$a_x = g\sin\theta - \mu g\cos\theta.$$ **[1]**

The glider has initial velocity $v$ at time $t = 0$. The displacement of the glider and point LP at any time is given by

$$x_{LP} = vt + \tfrac{1}{2}a_x t^2$$ **[1]**

$$x_{LP} = vt + \tfrac{1}{2}(g\sin\theta - \mu g\cos\theta)t^2$$ **[1]**

The only force acting on the projectile is gravity. The projectile moves in two dimensions both parallel to the plane and perpendicular to it. The projectile has acceleration components

$a_x = g\sin\theta \qquad a_y = -g\cos\theta$ **[2]**

and initial velocity components $\quad v_x = v \qquad v_y = v_o$ **[2]**

Its $x$ and $y$ displacements are given by $\quad x = vt + \tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta t^2 \qquad y = v_o t - \tfrac{1}{2}g\cos\theta t^2$ **[2]**

The $x$-displacement of the projectile relative to point LP is

$$\Delta x = x - x_{LP} = vt + \tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta t^2 - \left[vt + \tfrac{1}{2}(g\sin\theta - \mu g\cos\theta)t^2\right] = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu g\cos\theta t^2$$ **[2]**

When the projectile lands, $\quad y = 0$ **[1]**

$$0 = v_o t - \tfrac{1}{2}g\cos\theta t^2$$

Solving for $t$ and assuming $t \ne 0$

$$t = \frac{2v_o}{g\cos\theta}$$ **[1]**

$$\Delta x = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu g\cos\theta\left(\frac{2v_o}{g\cos\theta}\right)^2 = \frac{2\mu v_o^{\,2}}{g\cos\theta}$$ **[1]**

**b.** If the air is on the system can be assumed to be frictionless, $\mu = 0$. **[1]**

$$\Delta x = 0$$ **[4]**

The projectile lands at LP.

figures.alt: Force components on the glider: two crossed arrows; one along the plane with ends labelled f_k=μF_N (up the slope) and mg sin θ (down the slope), the other perpendicular to the plane with ends labelled F_N (outward) and mg cos θ (into the plane); the angle θ is marked below.

problems.statement:
A wooden 45° right triangle has uniform mass $M$ and two equal sides of length $L$. The coordinates of the triangle’s center of gravity, measured with respect to the axes shown in Fig. 4-1 above, are

$$x_{cg} = L/3 \qquad\qquad y_{cg} = L/3.$$

The triangle is placed on a rough horizontal surface and a horizontal force is applied at the top of the triangle, as shown in Fig. 4-2. The force is gradually increased until the triangle just starts to tip over without sliding. The force is then removed and the surface is inclined as shown in Fig 4-3. The triangle is placed on the inclined plane. For what range of angle $\theta$, measured with respect to the horizontal, can you be certain that the triangle will not slide?

figures.caption: Fig. 4-1
figures.alt: A right isosceles triangle with its right angle at the origin of x–y axes; both legs have length L, marked by grey double arrows along the y axis and the x axis.

figures.caption: Fig. 4-2
figures.alt: The same right triangle standing on a horizontal surface with its vertical leg on the left; a horizontal arrow at the top vertex points to the left.

figures.caption: Fig. 4-3
figures.alt: The triangle resting with its hypotenuse-side leg on a plane inclined at angle θ to the horizontal, the angle θ marked at the lower right.

answer.note: The official solution prints “θ ≤ tan⁻¹(x_cg/L) − tan⁻¹(1/3) = 0.32 radians = 18.4°”; the minus sign between the two arctangents is evidently a misprint for “=”.

solution.statement:
**4.** Let $F$ be the magnitude of the horizontal force when the triangle just starts to tip over. The forces acting on the triangle when it is on the horizontal surface are shown in Figure 4-4.

Each force identified 1 point. **[4]**

Since the triangle is just starting to tip over and is not sliding, the conditions of static equilibrium still apply and, in addition, $\quad f_s \le \mu F_N.$ **[1]**

*(Students should not be penalized for using “=” instead of “$\le$” in intermediate steps. Finding the upper limit of the range is a valid technique.)*

The forces in the $x$-direction must sum to zero. $\quad F = f_s \le \mu F_N$ **[1]**

The forces in the $y$-direction must sum to zero. $\quad F_N = W$ **[1]**

The sum of the torques must also be zero. Taking torques about the lower left-hand corner,

$$0 = \sum \tau_i$$ **[1]**

Each torque can be written $\quad \tau_i = R_i F_i \sin\theta_i, \quad$ or $\quad \tau_i = R_{\perp i} F_i$ **[1]**

where $R_{\perp i}$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to line of action of the force.

$$0 = \sum \tau_i = FL - x_{cg}W$$ **[2]**

$$x_{cg}W = FL \le \mu WL$$ **[1]**

$$\mu \ge x_{cg}/L$$ **[1]**

$$\mu \ge 1/3$$ **[1]**

Let $\theta_m$ be the maximum inclination angle for which the triangle will not slide. The parallel and perpendicular components of the forces acting on the triangle are shown in Figure 4-5.

Each correct force component 1 point. **[4]**

The components perpendicular to the plane must sum to zero. $\quad F_N = W\cos\theta_m$ **[1]**

The components parallel to the plane must sum to zero. $\quad \mu F_N = W\sin\theta_m.$ **[1]**

Combining the last two equations: $\quad W\sin\theta_m = \mu W\cos\theta_m$

$$\tan\theta_m = \mu \ge x_{cg}/L$$ **[1]**

We can only be certain that $\theta_m$ is no smaller than $\quad \theta_m = \tan^{-1}\left(x_{cg}/L\right)$ **[1]**

The range we can be certain of has $\theta_m$ as its maximum

$$\theta \le \tan^{-1}\left(x_{cg}/L\right) - \tan^{-1}(1/3) = 0.32\ \text{radians} = 18.4^{\circ}$$ **[3]**

*$\{$Must have inequality for the full 3 points. Only one point for “=” instead of “$\le$”.$\}$*

figures.caption: Figure 4-4
figures.alt: Force diagram of the triangle on the horizontal surface (dashed outline): horizontal force F pointing left at the top vertex, normal force F_N upward at the lower left corner, static friction f_s pointing right along the base, weight W downward at horizontal distance x_cg from the left leg; the left leg is labelled L.

figures.caption: Figure 4-5
figures.alt: Force components for the triangle on the incline: two crossed arrows; along the plane f_s=μF_N (up the slope) and W sin θ_m (down the slope), perpendicular to the plane F_N (outward) and W cos θ_m (into the plane); the angle θ_m is marked below.
